runs.t: Chapter 1: Getting Started with Red Hat Enterprise Linux
Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I | Study file

This chapter explains what Linux is and why people use it. It also explains open source, Linux distributions, and where Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) fits in. There are almost no commands yet. First you learn the big ideas.
Topics in this chapter, in book order:
1.1 Why should you learn about Linux?
Linux quietly runs a huge part of the technology around you, so IT workers need to know it.

Think of the wiring inside a building. You rarely see it, but almost everything depends on it. Linux is like that wiring. Web shops, stock markets, smart TVs, in-flight screens, cloud services and most of the top 500 supercomputers run on it.
The book gives these reasons to learn it. Windows users must work with Linux systems. Applications and cloud machines often run on Linux. Phones and the
, meaning everyday devices connected to the internet, often use it. And Linux skills are in demand.
Linux is everywhere behind the scenes, so the skill is valuable.
Linux is great because it is open source, has a strong command line, and is modular.
Think of a set of building blocks where the plans are public and you can swap, add or remove any block.
: anyone can see how it works, change it and share the change. Improvements arrive faster.
. You control the computer by typing commands instead of clicking. Linux was built so that every admin task can be done this way. This makes
(letting the computer repeat tasks for you) and remote work easier.
. You can replace or remove parts. The same system can be a full desktop for developers or a tiny, stripped-down appliance, which is a device that does one job.

To check it worked: the same text appears on the next line.
Linux is open, command-line driven and modular.
Open source software is software whose source code anyone can use, study, change and share.
is the human-readable list of instructions that makes a program. Think of a cooking recipe.
(closed source) software gives you only the finished dish. You can eat it, but you cannot see or change the recipe.
Open source gives you the recipe too. The creator still owns the copyright, but a
(written permission) lets you run, read, change and pass on the code. It is
, meaning no fee for each copy.
Open source is not the same as "not commercial". Companies sell open source products and services. Red Hat, for example, sells help with using and supporting open source software.
Closed source:  you get the finished program only
Open source:    you get the program AND its source code
you can see what the code does and improve it.
you can learn from real code.
you can inspect sensitive code and fix it, with or without the original developers.
the code can survive if the original developer or company disappears.
Open source means you get the recipe, not only the dish.
All open source licenses let you use, view, change and share the code, but they differ in what they ask in return.
Think of lending a recipe. One lender says: "Copy it and improve it, but you must pass on the same freedom." Another says: "Do what you like, just keep my name on it."
(also called "share-alike"). Anyone who shares the code, changed or not, must also let others copy, change and share it. This keeps the code and its improvements open.
. You can use the code for any purpose if you keep the copyright and license notice. You may even put it inside closed products. This makes reuse easy, but improvements may end up proprietary-only.
Hundreds of licenses exist. These two groups are the important ones.
Permissive:  MIT/X11, Simplified BSD, Apache Software License 2.0
is the GNU General Public License.
is the Lesser GNU Public License.
Copyleft keeps code open; permissive makes code easy to reuse.
Most open source software today is built by paid professionals, with volunteers and universities helping.
Think of a community garden. Some gardeners are hired by local shops, and others volunteer. Both make the garden grow.

It is a misconception that open source comes only from an "army of volunteers". Many developers are paid by their companies to build the improvements their customers need. Volunteers and academics matter most in new technology areas. The mix of formal and informal work makes development lively and productive.
Open source development today is overwhelmingly professional, helped by volunteers.
Red Hat is a company that helps customers use open source software.
Think of a travel agent between you and a huge, busy city. Red Hat sits between customers and the open source community, and helps them connect and work well together.

Red Hat takes an active part in open source communities and believes open source is the future of IT. It is best known for the Linux community and for Red Hat Enterprise Linux. It also works in other areas such as virtualization, cloud, middleware and storage.
Red Hat helps customers connect with the open source community.
A Linux distribution is a ready-to-install operating system built around the Linux kernel plus many other programs.

Think of a car. The engine comes from one maker, the seats from another, the wheels from a third. A distribution is the finished car, already put together and tested. (The comparison stops here: a car's parts have one buyer, but Linux parts come from many independent communities.)

, the software that manages the computer. It controls hardware, memory and which programs run. In 1991, a student named Linus Torvalds wrote the Linux kernel and shared it as open source under the GPL.
A kernel alone is not enough. It needs tools, a graphical interface and servers from other projects. Collecting all those pieces was hard, so

Common traits of distributions: a kernel plus user programs; small or very large; a way to install and update; a provider who supports it.
A distribution is a kernel plus programs, packaged so you can install and update it easily.
1.8 Development of Red Hat Enterprise Linux
Red Hat improves open source projects, tests them in Fedora, then stabilizes them for RHEL.

Think of a restaurant with a test kitchen. New dishes are tried in the test kitchen first. The ones that work go on the main menu. (The comparison stops here: Fedora is not private. It is public and free for anyone.)
There are three steps. First, Red Hat supports individual open source projects. These are called
projects, the places where the original code is developed. Red Hat gives code, developer time and resources, often working with other Linux distributions.
Second, Red Hat sponsors and combines projects into
, a community Linux. Fedora is the proving ground for new features.
Third, Red Hat stabilizes the software for long-term support and builds it into RHEL.
Upstream projects  ->  Fedora       ->  Red Hat Enterprise Linux
means "the work moves on to the next stage".
Upstream is where code starts; Fedora is the fast-moving test area; RHEL is the stable, supported result.
RHEL is built from open source work that is first proven in Fedora.
Fedora is a free community Linux that focuses on new ideas, not long life.

Think of a fashion show: the newest designs, changing often. Red Hat sponsors Fedora and works with its community. Everything Fedora makes goes back to the free and open source world, and anyone can take part.

The book says Fedora has a major update about every six months, and updates can bring big changes. A release is supported for only about a year. That makes it less suitable for enterprise use, where systems must stay stable for years.
Fedora is fast and new; it is not built for long-term stability.
RHEL is Red Hat's commercially supported Linux distribution, and you pay a subscription for support, not for the code.
Think of a service plan for a car. The engine design is open for anyone to read. You pay the garage for guaranteed repairs, updates and experts who answer when you call.
RHEL is tested a lot and has a large ecosystem: partners, hardware and software certifications, consulting, training and support for many years.

Red Hat bases each major release on Fedora. After that, Red Hat picks which packages to include, makes improvements (sent back to upstream projects and Fedora), and sets configuration choices for customers.
is the payment model. It is not a license fee, because the software is open source. When a new major release arrives, customers can move to it when they like, at no extra cost.
Code:          free to read, change and share
Subscription:  support, maintenance, updates, security patches,
Knowledgebase on the Red Hat Customer Portal,
is Red Hat's support website, at
is its library of help articles for subscribers.
With RHEL you pay for long-term support and expertise, not for the software code.
RHEL 8.0 is the release this book teaches, with its own support phases (the book mentions a Maintenance Support 2 phase).
Red Hat's life cycle page now covers RHEL 8, 9 and 10. Each has a ten-year life cycle made of three phases: Full Support, Maintenance Support and Extended Life Phase.
Red Hat Enterprise Linux Life Cycle, https://access.redhat.com/node/493203, checked 2026-10-16.
CentOS, as the book describes it, is a free, community-run Linux made from much of RHEL's code, with no vendor support.
Think of a store-brand copy of a well-known recipe. It uses the same main ingredients and costs nothing. But there is no help desk you can call.
Volunteers support CentOS, independent of Red Hat. It is free and easy to install. The book lists these key differences from RHEL.
Support:        CentOS self-support / RHEL paid levels
Fixes:          CentOS waits / RHEL may hot-fix first
Certification:  CentOS rarely / RHEL thousands of apps
CentOS is self-support. RHEL has several support levels, such as business hours or 24x7 for critical issues.
CentOS errata (official fix releases) start only after RHEL releases them. RHEL developers can respond faster.
vendors like SAS, SAP and Oracle generally do not certify CentOS.
CentOS uses forums, mailing lists and chat. RHEL has the Customer Portal and
, an optional online tool that checks your systems for risks.
CentOS is free but self-supported; RHEL adds support, certifications and fast fixes.
CentOS is a rebuild of much of the RHEL codebase.

The CentOS Project now describes CentOS Stream as a continuously delivered distribution that tracks just ahead of RHEL, between Fedora Linux and RHEL. Third-party sites (Linode, OpenLogic) report that CentOS Linux 8 ended at the end of 2021 and that all CentOS Linux versions ended on June 30, 2024. NOT VERIFIED on an official page.

CentOS Stream, https://www.centos.org/centos-stream/, checked 2026-10-16. To confirm the CentOS Linux end dates, check centos.org and Red Hat's FAQ: https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/faq-centos-stream-updates.
1.12 Trying Out Red Hat Enterprise Linux
You can try RHEL through an evaluation download, a free developer subscription, or a cloud instance.
Think of a test drive before you buy. The book lists three ways.

One: download an evaluation copy from Red Hat's website. Two: join the Red Hat Developer Program, which offers free subscriptions for developing, testing and demonstrating software. Three: start a RHEL
(a virtual machine that runs in a provider's data center) at a cloud provider. For example, Red Hat has official
(ready-made machine images) in the Amazon AWS Marketplace.
You can try RHEL by download, developer subscription, or the cloud.
The evaluation page, the Red Hat Developer Program and the AWS Marketplace images are available at the addresses the book gives.
NOT VERIFIED. I did not check these programs or addresses.
To check: Red Hat's "Get Started with Red Hat Enterprise Linux" page and https://developer.redhat.com. Not checked on 2026-10-16.
Get Started with Red Hat Enterprise Linux (https://access.redhat.com/products/red-hat-enterprise-linux#getstarted) and The Open Source Way (https://opensource.com/open-source-way).

A small company wants to run its online shop on Linux. They like open source because they can read the code and are not locked in. Their developers try new ideas on Fedora. For the real shop they choose RHEL, because they want years of tested software and expert support. Their admin runs it from the command line.
Open source code  ->  a distribution packages it  ->  RHEL adds testing and a support subscription
